title: Kernel Representation and Similarity Measure for Incomplete Data
summary: Measuring similarity between samples with missing values usually forces row deletion or imputation as a separate preprocessing step, which loses information and biases downstream tasks such as clustering. The paper proposes the proximity kernel: per-feature equal-frequency (percentile) bin centers with nearest-center (Voronoi) assignment and one-hot encoding into a sparse d×nbins space, where missing features are estimated as bin-probability distributions via a three-level cascading fallback (intersection matching → union matching → global priors) using kernel mean embedding, and similarity is the normalized inner product K=(1/d)z^T z'. Averaged over 10 runs of K-means (k = ground-truth class count) on 12 UCI incomplete datasets, it reaches 0.4245 mean NMI versus 0.3773 for the best baseline (HI-PMK), is best or second-best on 10 of 12 datasets, and scores 0.2289 NMI on Hepatitis.

match_target.why: The user's target hint is exactly this cell (Table 3, proximity kernel NMI on Hepatitis, K-means). It is the cheapest demonstration of the paper's central claim that the kernel representation beats impute-then-cluster baselines: 155-sample dataset, CPU-only, no iterative training, deterministic pipeline aside from K-means init.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: NMI is a bounded score and the Hepatitis set has only 155 examples (<2,000), so the band is 2.0 points; the paper prints NMI as a fraction in [0,1] (0.2289), so 0.02 in fraction units. The paper reports only a 10-run mean with no std/CI, so rule 1 does not apply.

requirements.stmt: Per feature, compute nbins bin centers as evenly-spaced percentiles of the observed (non-missing) values only: c_{j,k} = percentile(X_obs,j, (k-1)*100/(nbins-1)), k=1..nbins, so the first and last centers equal the feature min and max.
requirements.quote: The bin centers cj,kare determined by computing evenly-spaced percentiles of the observed distribution:

requirements.stmt: Assign each observed value to its NEAREST bin center (argmin over centers, Eq. 5), i.e. Voronoi proximity assignment — NOT classic interval-membership binning; this is what produces the density-adaptive cells.
requirements.quote: Unlike traditional binning methods that assign values to bins based on interval membership, our approach employs proximity assignment.

requirements.stmt: One-hot encode the bin assignment of each feature (binary vector of length nbins) and concatenate across all features to get z_i of length d*nbins; complete samples have exactly d ones.
requirements.quote: The complete encoding for sample iconcatenates the one-hot vectors across all features as:

requirements.stmt: Missing handling Level 1: per observed feature j build C_{i,j} = {m : m != i, b_{m,j} = b_{i,j}}, take the intersection S1(i) over ALL observed features; if S1(i) is non-empty, set the missing features' encodings to the average one-hot over S1(i) (KME).
requirements.quote: If S1(i) ≠∅, we estimate missing encoding through kernel mean embedding:

requirements.stmt: Level 2 fallback: if S1(i) is empty, use the union S2(i) of C_{i,j} over observed features (samples sharing at least one bin on any observed feature) and average their one-hot encodings.
requirements.quote: we relax the constraint to consider samples that match on any observed feature.

requirements.stmt: Level 3 fallback: if S2(i) is empty, set the missing feature's encoding to the global bin prior p_{j,k} = count(samples in bin k for feature j) / count(samples with observed feature j), which sums to 1.
requirements.quote: we cannot leverage local similarity and must use the global distribution of each missing feature.

requirements.stmt: Define the kernel K(x_m,x_n) = (1/d) z_m^T z_n and use the representation z_i directly as input features for K-means with k set to the ground-truth number of classes; evaluate with NMI.
requirements.quote: For fair comparison, we applied K-means with the number of clusters to the ground-truth number of classes.

requirements.stmt: Every reported cell is the average of 10 repeated experiments; reproduce with 10 repetitions and report the mean.
requirements.quote: Each experiment was conducted 10 times and report average results for stability.

requirements.stmt: The method's single hyperparameter, bins per dimension, must be searched over {2,3,4,6,8} for the main-table results; the paper also reports stability for nbins in 2-10 and recommends 3-6 in practice.
requirements.quote: For the proximity kernel, we search the number of bins per dimension in {2, 3, 4, 6, 8}.

requirements.stmt: Evaluate on the 12 UCI datasets of Table 2 with their NATIVE missingness (no synthetic masking for Table 3; synthetic MCAR 10-50% is used only in §5.3 on 3L and Messidor). Hepatitis must be 155x19, 13 categorical + 6 numerical, 5.67% missing, 2 classes.
requirements.quote: We evaluate the proximity kernel on 12 real-world datasets with varying characteristics.

requirements.stmt: If reproducing the full comparison table: baselines are Mean, MissForest, MICE, KNN, EM (scikit-learn) and GAIN, MIRACLE, MIWAE, HI-PMK (hyperimpute), each with the paper's stated hyperparameter grids.
requirements.quote: The code of them are from python library scikit-learn 2 and hyperimpute 3 [10].

requirements.stmt: Clustering on z_i is kernel k-means with the PSD kernel K = (1/d) Z Z^T; a plain K-means on z_i is an equivalent implementation because the objective depends only on K(x_i,x_j).
requirements.quote: Expanding the squared distance shows that this objective depends on kernel values K(xi,xj), making k-means in representation space equivalent to a kernel-based clustering approach.
